strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: its profiling identifies the LLM as over 70% of OpenVLA-OFT inference latency, making visual-token pruning potentially useful for real-time robotic control.
The combination of temporal information, early-layer attention, dynamic scene changes, and action granularity is intuitively motivated and represents a useful synthesis of existing pruning ideas.

Evaluation covers all four LIBERO suites, reportedly using 40–50 trials per task, and measures end-to-end latency on both A800 and RTX 3090 GPUs. The reported 1.46x and 1.57x average speedups with nearly unchanged aggregate success rates are promising.

The component ablation suggests that the action-aware controller can recover success rate at little latency cost. Visualizations also provide qualitative evidence that retained patches often cover manipulated objects and robot geometry.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes an honest discussion of the simulation-to-reality limitation. The simulation-only experiments raise no immediate research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The method is not reproducible from the manuscript. Essential parameters are missing, including KG, KD, the similarity threshold tau, rank-decay coefficient k, velocity thresholds, epsilon, Q, and the layer-update and layer-pruning sets. Initialization for the first action and behavior when fewer than KD patches pass the threshold are also unspecified, and no code-release statement is provided.

The pruning-ratio specification is internally contradictory. Section 7.1 assigns alpha=1.0 to Spatial and 0.6 to Long, whereas Appendix 10.2 assigns 0.6 to Spatial and 1.0 to Long. Moreover, the text and Table 3 say larger alpha prunes more tokens, while Algorithm 1 and the appendix define retained-token counts as proportional to alpha, which implies the opposite behavior.

The central attention score is problematic as written. Equation 1 defines attention from a visual-token query to text tokens. In the decoder-only Llama2 backbone, visual tokens conventionally precede text tokens, so causal masking prevents such visual-to-later-text attention; task relevance normally uses text/action queries attending to visual keys. This directionality ambiguity affects the central global and local selection mechanisms.

The proposed layer confidence mu_attn/(sigma_attn+epsilon) lacks justification. Attention rows are normalized, making their mean largely determined by sequence length, while nearly uniform and therefore uninformative attention has very small variance and can receive maximal confidence. No comparison against simpler attention aggregation is supplied.

Evidence for the motivating claims is too informal. Figure 3 is described only as using “some tasks,” with no task list, trial count, uncertainty, or protocol details. Figure 5 likewise omits its evaluation population and precise hit-rate denominator; taking a union of top-k sets from multiple layers also mechanically increases coverage, so the claimed 85–95% predictiveness is not established convincingly.

The main success-rate comparisons report no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or paired significance tests. With only 40–50 rollouts per task, sub-percentage differences such as 97.6% versus 98.2% cannot support claims of improvement or equivalence without uncertainty analysis. The exact rollout count is itself given only as a range.

The complexity analysis contains serious inconsistencies. Its Transformer FLOP expression uses a 2LDM term with M defined as the number of attention heads, omitting the usual feed-forward width dependence. Four 10% pruning events would not yield the stated 0.81 factor under straightforward cumulative pruning, and the derivation mixes 0.9, a claimed 19% average reduction, and 0.81 without explanation.

Baseline fairness and timing reproducibility are insufficient. EfficientVLA is an unofficial reimplementation originally designed for another action architecture, but validation against the original implementation is absent. Precision, batching, software versions, warm-up, synchronization, number of timing runs, and overhead attributable to attention extraction and frame comparison are not reported.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the conclusions: only OpenVLA-OFT and LIBERO simulation are evaluated, and both hardware platforms are NVIDIA GPUs. This does not establish model-architecture generality, real-world robustness, or broad hardware generalization. Temporal pruning may also fail under camera motion, occlusion, abrupt scene changes, or controller stalls, none of which is stress-tested.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: temporal reuse, frame-difference selection, early-layer token scoring, layerwise pruning, and velocity-gated computation are established ideas combined through several heuristics. Calling the approach “self-speculative” is potentially misleading because it lacks the proposal-and-verification/correction mechanism normally central to speculative inference.

Presentation has numerous consequential ambiguities and naming inconsistencies, including OpenVLA-OPT versus OpenVLA-OFT, “action adapter” versus controller, conflicting Pt-1 versus It-T comparisons in Algorithm 1, and equations that return similarity scores where token sets are required. These issues go beyond cosmetic writing problems because they obscure the implemented algorithm.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges simulation-only evaluation but omits important deployment risks: pruning-induced rare control errors, reliance on velocity as a proxy for manipulation precision, misclassification of idle or failed states as fine control, and the safety implications of using an approximate policy on physical robots.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant bottleneck: visual-token computation dominates OpenVLA-OFT inference, and exploiting temporal redundancy between consecutive observations is a reasonable direction.

The proposed system combines temporal attention reuse, change-based token preservation, layer-wise pruning, and action-sensitive pruning in a training-free framework. The reported LIBERO results cover four suites, 40–50 trials per task, and two GPUs; Table 1 reports a 1.46× average A800 speedup while largely preserving success rates.

The evaluation includes competing pruning/caching baselines, a limited component ablation, design-space exploration, latency/FLOP reporting, and visualizations of retained patches. The manuscript is visually clear and includes an explicit simulation-to-reality limitation. weaknesses: Soundness: the action-aware controller appears causally ill-defined. Algorithm 1 computes the current action's translational and rotational velocities before static pruning and model inference, although those velocities are outputs of that inference. If previous-action velocity is actually used, the method and equations need to state this and evaluate the resulting lag. This ambiguity affects a central component credited with restoring success rate.

Soundness and presentation: the attention equation uses A(V_i,t_j), described as attention from a visual token to text tokens. In a causal decoder such as the Llama-based OpenVLA-OFT, visual tokens ordinarily cannot attend to later instruction tokens; task-to-visual attention would instead be A(t_j,V_i). Thus either the central importance score is written in the wrong direction or the required attention structure is unexplained.

The experimental configuration is internally inconsistent. Section 7.1 assigns alpha values of Spatial=1.0, Goal=0.8, Object=0.6, and Long=0.6, whereas Appendix 10.2 states Spatial=0.6, Goal=0.8, Object=0.6, and Long=1.0. Moreover, Algorithm 1 and the appendix define retained-token counts as increasing with alpha, but Section 7.4 and Table 3 say that increasing alpha prunes more tokens. These contradictions prevent reliable interpretation or reproduction of the headline results.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Crucial quantities are not specified, including K_G, K_D, tau, rank-sigmoid parameter k, all velocity thresholds, Q, and the precise update/pruning layer sets. Patch features used for cosine similarity, initialization at the first action, handling of the two camera streams, timing protocol, precision, synchronization, warm-up, software versions, and random seeds are also absent. No code or artifact is provided.

The FLOP analysis is not trustworthy. Its per-layer formula uses M as the number of heads in a 2LDM term while omitting the usual dominant feed-forward-network cost; its subsequent calculation applies unexplained factors. The appendix suggests approximately 63% FLOP reduction, while Table 1 reports 43% FLOPs remaining, and the claim that four 10% pruning events reduce token count by 19% across all layers is not derived correctly. This weakens the compute-bound motivation and efficiency claims.

The evidence does not isolate why the method works. The ablation uses only LIBERO-Spatial, labels components merely as “Tech.1/2/3,” and adds them cumulatively; it does not separately test previous-step global attention, frame differencing, early-layer local attention, rank/confidence scoring, velocity-based frame selection, or each controller condition. There are no simple temporal-pruning controls, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests, so small differences such as 98.2% versus 97.6% may be sampling noise.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. EfficientVLA is reimplemented because its code is unavailable and is adapted from a different action-expert setting, but the paper provides no validation that the reproduction matches published behavior. Dataset-specific pruning ratios appear selected using benchmark success rates without a separate validation protocol, creating a risk of test-set tuning. Comparisons are limited to one VLA backbone and one simulation benchmark.

Originality and significance are moderate rather than strong: the contribution is primarily a combination of existing attention-based pruning, temporal reuse, and handcrafted velocity heuristics. Evaluation on only OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO does not establish robustness to camera motion, distribution shift, other VLA architectures, real-time control behavior, or physical robots. Claims of generalization are therefore too broad; testing two NVIDIA GPUs supports hardware portability, not model or environment generalization.

Presentation contains additional consequential ambiguities: the claimed pruning “at the beginning” conflicts with requiring two full early layers for local selection; the set expression for V_prune lacks parentheses and, literally, unions retained dynamic/local tokens into the prune set; Equation 3 appears to return similarity values rather than tokens; and the velocity-based frame-offset formula is unexplained and lacks a stated valid velocity range. The limitations section acknowledges simulation-only evaluation but omits these methodological fragilities and potential physical-control safety implications.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important practical bottleneck: reducing end-to-end VLA inference latency without retraining. Combining temporal attention reuse, change-based token retention, layer-wise pruning, and action-sensitive pruning is intuitive and well motivated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/5d70eb02da6545d1b171b02849795ffa/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported gains are meaningful: relative to OpenVLA-OFT, SpecPrune-VLA averages 1.46× end-to-end speedup on A800 and 1.57× on RTX 3090 while maintaining similar LIBERO success rates. Evaluation spans all four LIBERO suites and two substantially different GPUs.

The paper provides useful diagnostic evidence, including early-versus-final-layer top-k overlap, pruning sensitivity, latency/FLOP breakdowns, retained-token visualizations, and a component-level ablation. These analyses make the proposed heuristics easier to understand.
The approach is training-free and targets the LLM bottleneck directly, making it potentially useful for existing VLA deployments.

The simulation-only limitation is stated honestly. The work involves no human-subject data or evident immediate ethical concern, although safety implications of deploying approximate policies on physical robots remain unexamined.
weaknesses: The method is not specified consistently enough to reproduce. Section 7.1 assigns alpha=1.0 to Spatial and 0.6 to Long, whereas Appendix 10.2 assigns alpha=0.6 to Spatial and 1.0 to Long. The latter appears more consistent with Table 4, but the manuscript never resolves the contradiction. Important quantities—including K_G, K_D, the similarity threshold, velocity thresholds, rank-decay constant, update/pruning layer sets, and Q in Algorithm 1—are also missing or ambiguous.

The action-aware controller has a temporal ambiguity central to soundness. It selects the pruning mode using translational and rotational velocity derived from a policy action, yet pruning is needed before that action is produced. The overview suggests that the previous action may be used, while the text and algorithm describe the current step. The exact causal procedure, first-step initialization, and any lag-induced failures need to be defined and tested.

Some mathematical definitions appear questionable or incomplete. Equation (1) uses attention from a visual token to text tokens, whereas task-relevance selection commonly requires text-query attention to visual keys; token ordering and masking are not explained. Patch features used for frame similarity are undefined. The FLOP formula defines M as the number of heads despite using it in an MLP-like term, and the appendix's claimed 63% reduction is not reconciled with the 43% remaining-FLOPs result in Table 1.

The evaluation does not establish statistical reliability. Although tasks are repeated 40–50 times, the exact number, random seeds, dispersion, and confidence intervals are absent. Consequently, sub-percentage success-rate differences—including the claimed negligible loss and apparent improvements—cannot be distinguished from sampling variation.

Pruning ratios are selected separately for each benchmark suite, apparently using success results from those same suites. This introduces possible test-set tuning and weakens the claim of an adaptive method. A fixed configuration, held-out tuning protocol, or sensitivity study across every suite is needed.

External validity is limited to one VLA backbone and one simulator. Testing two GPUs supports hardware portability, but not generalization across VLA architectures, observation distributions, or physical-robot noise. The limitations section acknowledges simulation but overlooks the single-model scope and deployment-safety implications.

The comparison with EfficientVLA is difficult to interpret because it is a reimplementation of an unavailable method originally designed for a different action architecture. The paper gives too little validation of that reimplementation for its large success-rate degradation to serve as strong comparative evidence.

The ablation is confined to LIBERO-Spatial and only adds components cumulatively. It does not isolate global-attention reuse, dynamic-frame supplementation, early-layer selection, the proposed confidence score, or velocity-based sampling, so the evidence does not show which novel ingredients are necessary.

Presentation is visually clear overall, but terminology and notation need substantial cleanup: the method is called “self-speculative” without a verification/correction mechanism analogous to speculative decoding, alpha is described both as a pruning ratio and a retained-token multiplier, and several equations, captions, and claims contain inconsistencies or grammatical errors. Given the promising empirical result but unresolved specification and evidential issues, revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The central hypothesis—reusing prior-step attention because consecutive robot observations are similar—is plausible and supported by reported 75–88% important-token overlap. Component ablations show benefits from global-attention reuse, entropy weighting, and the action-aware controller.
Significance: The reported efficiency gains are practically meaningful: 1.46× end-to-end speedup with OpenVLA-OFT, 1.31× with π0, and 1.70× on real-robot tasks, alongside substantial FLOP reductions.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover four LIBERO suites, LIBERO-plus perturbations, two VLA architectures, A800/RTX 3090 hardware, and four real-world tasks. Comparisons include several pruning and caching baselines.

Originality: Combining cross-timestep attention reuse, early-layer local selection, progressive layer-wise pruning, and velocity-conditioned pruning is a useful training-free synthesis, even though its individual ingredients are largely heuristic extensions of prior pruning methods.
Presentation: The paper provides equations, an algorithm, component ablations, complexity analysis, latency breakdowns, parameter settings, and real-world training details.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of 'negligible' success-rate degradation is not statistically established. The paper omits the number of evaluation rollouts and gives no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests. Table 12 reports an unspecified number of seeds using half-range rather than standard deviation or standard error, so differences such as 96.8% versus 96.4% cannot be interpreted reliably.

Reproducibility: No code or implementation release is identified, and important protocol details are missing, including rollout counts, exact seeds, latency repetitions, warm-up and synchronization procedure, numerical precision, batch size, handling of the first timestep when prior attention is unavailable, and behavior when fewer than Kdynamic patches pass the threshold.

Method specification contains inconsistencies. Equation 2 scores visual-query-to-text-key attention, whereas Equation 7 switches to text-query-to-image-key attention while using the same 'image-to-text' terminology. Entropy is computed on an image-only slice without stated renormalization, so a low value can reflect little total image attention rather than a concentrated distribution. The mapping of tokens across views/dual visual encoders and some layer-pruning details are also unclear.

The broad generalization claim is overstated. Fixed thresholds and constants—including velocity thresholds, frame-lag parameters, top-K values, and pruning depths—are selected empirically, largely on LIBERO. Normalized actions do not inherently make velocity thresholds independent of robot kinematics, and the UniVLA/SimplerEnv discussion shows velocity profiles rather than task-performance evidence for the complete method.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. EfficientVLA is only partially reimplemented because its code is unavailable, while tuning details for several other baselines are sparse. The π0 study includes no competing acceleration methods, limiting evidence that the approach generalizes competitively beyond OpenVLA-OFT.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: prior-step caching, attention-based token pruning, progressive pruning, and confidence-based controllers are established ideas. The term 'self-speculative' is somewhat misleading because the method does not provide a speculative verification or correction mechanism analogous to speculative decoding.

Presentation needs substantial polishing: there are frequent grammatical errors, inconsistent figure references and terminology, duplicated appendix material, and mislabeled discussion around Tables 11–12. These issues make an already multi-stage heuristic pipeline harder to verify.

Limitations and ethics are inadequately treated. There is no dedicated limitations discussion covering temporal-discontinuity failures, camera motion, distribution shift, controller lag, or cases where prior attention becomes stale. The real-robot study also does not discuss safety procedures or failure consequences; while no major ethical violation is evident, this omission matters for deployment-oriented claims.

strengths: Soundness: The paper targets a genuine systems bottleneck and presents a plausible combination of temporal attention reuse, early-layer token selection, progressive pruning, and action-dependent pruning. Component ablations attribute gains to global attention reuse and entropy weighting rather than reporting only an end-to-end result.

Significance: If independently reproduced, reducing OpenVLA-OFT latency from 109.0 ms to about 75.1 ms while retaining similar LIBERO success would be useful for robotic control. Evaluation spans four LIBERO suites, LIBERO-Plus perturbations, two VLA architectures, two GPU classes, and four physical-robot tasks.

Presentation: The high-level motivation and system structure are understandable, and the rendered figures generally communicate the temporal-consistency intuition and speed–success trade-off effectively.

Originality: Reusing prior-step global attention as a pruning prior and modulating pruning according to inferred action granularity are sensible VLA-specific extensions beyond conventional single-step visual-token pruning.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central attention definition is internally inconsistent. Equation 2 ranks visual-query-to-text-key attention, whereas Equation 7 instead describes text-query-to-image-key attention while calling it image-to-text attention. In a causal VLA backbone, direction and token ordering determine whether these entries even exist. This ambiguity affects global selection, local selection, entropy weighting, and hence essentially the entire method.

Soundness/reproducibility: Several indispensable implementation details are absent or contradictory. The slope k in Equation 6 is unspecified; aggregation of layer-15 and layer-32 scores into V_global is unclear; first-step behavior is not defined; the source of the patch feature vectors used for frame similarity is ambiguous; and Algorithm 1 does not explicitly implement the mode-dependent K values. Moreover, the fixed 32-layer schedule and layers 15/32 are described for OpenVLA-OFT without specifying the corresponding schedule for the structurally different pi0 model.

Evidence: The claimed negligible accuracy loss is not established statistically. The paper gives no rollout counts, number of seeds, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests for the principal tables. Appendix Table 12 reports an unspecified number of runs using half-range rather than standard uncertainty. Differences such as 96.6% versus 96.1% therefore cannot support an equivalence or negligible-loss claim.

Evidence: The physical-robot study does not report the number of evaluation trials, uncertainty, randomization protocol, or test-condition variation. It lists training demonstrations and episode lengths instead. Consequently, percentages such as 96.7% and 82.0% and the assertion of uncompromised real-world success are not auditable.

Internal consistency: Table 1 reports 43% FLOPs remaining, while Appendix A.3 derives 37% after dynamic pruning. The text correspondingly claims both 57% and 63% FLOP reduction. The latency breakdown also does not provide warm-up, precision, synchronization, repetition, or variance methodology, making the headline speedups difficult to reproduce.

Experimental design: Hyperparameters and controller thresholds are selected on the same benchmark suites used for the headline evaluation, with no clean validation/test separation. The generalization experiment says that 200 LIBERO-Plus tasks were 'chosen' without explaining sampling, and the action-controller generalization discussion shows a trajectory plot rather than quantitative results on the claimed additional model and robot.

Presentation: There are numerous cross-reference and specification errors: the main text refers to Figure 13 for an ablation displayed as Figure 8; it alternates between LIBERO-Long and LIBERO-10; Algorithm 1 appears to reverse the update/prune condition relative to its prose; and the description of dynamic-patch filtering is confusing because it first thresholds candidates and then refers to selecting from 'remaining' candidates. These are consequential ambiguities rather than merely cosmetic issues.

Originality/significance: The contribution is largely a heuristic composition of attention-based pruning, temporal reuse, entropy weighting, and velocity thresholds. The paper does not isolate whether the added complexity provides a compelling Pareto improvement over a carefully tuned simpler temporal or early-attention baseline; its strongest competing speedup is similar, and baseline reimplementation details are uneven.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript contains no substantive limitations discussion. It does not address failure modes under abrupt scene changes, occlusion, camera motion, distribution shift, or errors in coarse/fine action classification. Although the ethical risk is limited, physical-robot experiments warrant at least a brief discussion of safety procedures and the risk that pruning-induced action errors could cause collisions or damage. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

strengths: Soundness: The central efficiency claim is supported across two substantially different VLA architectures. SpecPrune-VLA reports 1.46× end-to-end speedup with OpenVLA-OFT and 1.31× with π0 on LIBERO, while average success rates decrease by only 0.5 and 0.7 percentage points, respectively.

The ablations support important design choices: global-attention reuse improves token recall from 84% to 92% and LIBERO success from 93.4% to 96.1%; entropy-based layer weighting improves recall from 66% to 88% and success from 92.0% to 96.1%. Component and pruning-ratio ablations also expose the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Significance: Reducing VLA latency without retraining is practically valuable. The reported gains extend beyond one accelerator, reaching 1.57× end-to-end speedup on an RTX 3090 and 1.70× in four real-robot tasks on an RTX 4090.

Originality: Reusing prior-step deep attention as a temporal importance prior, supplementing it with changed patches and early-layer evidence, and modulating pruning using action granularity form a useful VLA-specific synthesis. The temporal-reuse idea is particularly well motivated by the measured 75–88% overlap of important tokens across consecutive observations.

The evaluation is broader than is typical for an inference paper: four standard LIBERO suites, LIBERO-plus perturbations, two model families, multiple GPUs, four real-world tasks, several pruning/caching baselines, visualizations, complexity analysis, and targeted ablations.
Presentation: The high-level pipeline and its motivation are generally easy to follow, and the main tables clearly communicate the practical speed-accuracy trade-off.
weaknesses: The evidence for “negligible” accuracy loss lacks adequate statistical support. The manuscript does not state the evaluation episode counts or number of random seeds, and reports half-ranges rather than standard deviations, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests. Real-world success percentages are likewise given without trial counts, making differences such as 85% versus 82% impossible to interpret reliably.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code-release statement, and latency measurements omit important details such as batch size, numerical precision, software/kernel versions, synchronization, warm-up, repetition count, and variability. Several baseline implementations and tuning choices are insufficiently specified; EfficientVLA is only partially reimplemented because its code is unavailable.

There are material specification inconsistencies. Section 4 defines importance using visual queries attending to text keys, whereas Section 5 describes text queries attending to image keys while using the same “image-to-text” terminology. Algorithm 1 updates scores only when a layer is not in the pruning set and otherwise prunes without incorporating that layer’s score, which does not clearly match the prose. Cold-start behavior for the first action is also unspecified.

The method relies on several empirically selected constants and architectural choices—layers 15 and 32, velocity thresholds, temporal-window formula, pruning layers, and top-K values—largely tuned on the evaluated environments. The claim that normalized actions make the controller independent of robot kinematics is stronger than the evidence, and full performance is not evaluated on the third robot/model used to illustrate threshold generalization.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but limited to four controlled tabletop tasks using task-specific fine-tuning. It does not test abrupt scene changes, camera failures, task switches, distractor motion, or recovery after an incorrectly classified fine-control phase, all of which directly challenge temporal attention reuse.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: most ingredients—attention-guided pruning, temporal reuse, entropy weighting, and heuristic adaptive sparsity—are established ideas. Moreover, “self-speculative” is potentially misleading because the method lacks the explicit draft-and-verification mechanism normally associated with speculative inference.

The paper has no substantive limitations or safety discussion. Since pruning errors concentrate around grasping and placement, the manuscript should discuss collision, object-dropping, and deployment safeguards for physical robots. There are also presentation issues, including inconsistent table values, mistaken cross-references, an incorrect Table 11 column label, and numerous grammatical errors.
